title: Trade, Foreign Investment, and Industrial Policy for Developing Countries
research_question: Do developing countries gain by abandoning policy neutrality with respect to trade, foreign investment, and the allocation of resources across industries? Specifically, are tariffs, subsidies, and tax breaks that go beyond optimal-tax or revenue considerations welfare-improving, and which forms of such intervention—if any—deliver higher productivity, growth, and structural transformation?
data_description: The chapter synthesizes evidence from roughly 200 prior empirical studies and presents original cross-country tabulations. Country-level data on trade policy come from World Bank and IMF sources covering 1980–2004, including statutory average tariffs, tariff revenues as a share of trade flows, tariff dispersion (standard deviations), nominal and real (Penn World Tables 6.1) trade shares in GDP, nominal exchange rates, and FDI inflows as a share of GDP, for both developing and high-income countries. The authors compute pairwise correlations among these openness indicators for the full sample and a developing-country subsample. The review also draws on industry-level case material (e.g., U.S. steel rails and tinplate, Japanese semiconductors, Brazilian microcomputers, Danish wind power, Airbus, Turkish manufacturing, Korean and Taiwanese sectors) and firm- and sector-level studies of FDI spillovers, learning-by-exporting, and productivity in developing economies.
institutional_context: Over the past three decades developing countries have substantially opened their markets to international trade and FDI, with average tariffs collapsing in places like India (from ~99% in 1980 to ~28% in 2004), Bangladesh, Costa Rica, China, Turkey, and Chile, and developing-country export shares overtaking those of high-income countries by the early 1990s. Yet most governments simultaneously pursued active interventions—export promotion, FDI tax incentives, subsidized credit, local-content rules, sectoral targeting, and selective tariff protection—motivated variously by infant-industry arguments, fiscal revenue needs, terms-of-trade considerations, and political pressures. East Asian successes (Korea, Taiwan, China) are often contrasted with Latin American import-substitution experiences. This setting raises the question of whether departures from policy neutrality—'hard' price-distorting measures versus 'soft' coordination-supporting policies—have been responsible for, or have impeded, observed productivity growth and structural transformation.
